Clarity.justification: The paper is well-structured with logical sections (Introduction, Related Work, Method, Results, Discussion), clear tables summarizing benchmark pairs and results, and figures illustrating rank correlations. Ideas such as partial Spearman ρ with MMLU control and the adversarial disruption hypothesis are articulated explicitly. Minor issues include dense technical prose and occasional inconsistencies between reported values (e.g., ρ_ANLI = 0.684) and code outputs, but overall coherence is high.

Novelty.justification: The work applies capability-controlled rank correlation (previously used in commonsense benchmarks) to trustworthiness dimensions and falsifies an N=2 observation from DecodingTrust at scale (N=13-16). This provides an empirical baseline for predictive validity of in-distribution trustworthiness rankings. However, the core question of rank stability across shifts is incremental rather than groundbreaking, and contributions remain within existing evaluation paradigms from TrustLLM and HELM.

Soundness.justification: Methods (partial Spearman ρ via pingouin, Fisher z-test, rank reversal counts) are appropriate, and raw-to-partial ρ contrast is well-motivated. Results are supported by published TrustLLM scores, with zero rank reversals and positive partial ρ values. However, preregistered criteria are not met (Δρ = 0.192 < 0.200), sensitivity to covariate choice collapses Δρ to 0.073 under Winogrande, N asymmetry (16 vs. 13) affects comparisons, and code/paper numerical mismatches (e.g., ρ values, two-sided vs. one-sided tests) indicate reliability concerns. Visualizations align with reported stability but highlight the near-miss on effect size.

Significance.justification: The paper addresses a practically important assumption for safety-sensitive LLM deployment: whether in-distribution benchmark rankings predict OOD behavior. Positive stability findings (fairness ρ=0.962; robustness ρ=0.684-0.868) support benchmark-based model selection, while falsifying the adversarial disruption hypothesis revises theoretical expectations. Impact is tempered by the unconfirmed directional advantage and open questions on mechanisms (latent bias vs. benchmark structure).

strengths: First large-scale (N=16) capability-controlled analysis of trustworthiness rank stability across fairness and robustness dimensions
Clear falsification of adversarial disruption hypothesis with zero rank reversals and positive partial correlations after MMLU control
weaknesses: Preregistered effect-size criterion (Δρ ≥ 0.200) not met (observed 0.192, p=0.024); directional claim remains unconfirmed
High sensitivity to capability covariate and N=13 subset for differential test reduce robustness of conclusions
